title: Keep precision diagnostics separate from the required reference
applies_when: Changing batching, reduction order or precision produces a numerical mismatch, especially near an argmax or another discrete decision boundary. Also applies when a boundary regression assigns new numerical semantics to an optional score_scale or another scalar.
lesson: Specify whether correctness means exact output identity, numerical tolerance or a statistical property. Localize the first divergence and compare both arms under that contract. Supplement random unit inputs with baseline-captured activations, learned weights, shapes and epsilon values; replay the unchanged candidate on those inputs before costly performance qualification. Verify that capture does not alter the baseline. A matching argmax does not satisfy a separately required full-output tolerance. A higher-precision side calculation can diagnose sensitivity, but candidate-only recomputation does not establish agreement with a stock low-precision baseline. Test a proposed selective fallback on held-out boundary cases and include detection and replay costs.
avoid_when: Do not impose exact token identity on every floating-point or stochastic operator. A small decision margin is a diagnostic clue, not a guarantee that selective recomputation is sufficient or profitable. Read whether a scale is a multiplier or divisor before defining its zero behavior. Optional[float] does not establish that zero is supported, nor that producing NaN/Inf is the correct fix. A before-fail/after-pass test of that newly chosen expectation needs an independent accepted contract or supported caller. An explicit documented zero-input contract can still justify a change; default-only callers do not prove all external uses safe.

evidence.note: PyTorch documents that mathematically equivalent operations and batched or individual computations need not agree bitwise. Activation replay and selective precision repair are workflow hypotheses, not measured cost benefits established by this source.
NVIDIA describes reference comparison using the criteria appropriate to the algorithm, including exactness or tolerance. It does not choose the current operator's contract.

The Torch QSA reference divides scores by score_scale or sqrt(head_dim); the decode reference and TileLang paths follow the same convention. Replacing the expression for zero would change the numerical contract, not merely distinguish None. Source evidence, not native/GPU validation or a universal zero-input policy.
These indexer prefill/decode calls omit the optional scale. They do not establish a zero-scale production failure or rule out an unobserved external caller.
